results.title: Meta's AI Agents Fail Due to Lack of Decision Data and Workflow Understanding | Vin Vashishta posted on the topic | LinkedIn
results.content:
Vin, “brittle mimics in broken workflows” is the most precise description of what bad AI deployment produces that I’ve seen.
The failure mode you’re describing at Meta is the same one playing out in PE-backed portfolio companies at a fraction of the scale — with far less runway to absorb the mistake.
Failure Mode 1 is the one that hits CFOs hardest. The decision logic that makes a business work — why that customer gets an exception, why that deal gets approved at that margin, why that variance gets escalated — lives in people’s heads, not in the keystroke log. You can’t extract judgment from action traces. You can only capture it through structured knowledge transfer before the person walks out the door. [...] Failure Mode 2: Pure automation misaligns with how agents create value.
Agents enable work to be done in completely new ways. New value can be created because agents scale in ways that people don’t. The workflow must be rebuilt, and people become more important than ever.
Keystrokes and mouse clicks cannot teach a business how to reorchestrate the workflow. Only experts can. ‘Replace the worker’ mandates produce brittle mimics in broken workflows.
‘Redesign the capability’ approaches produce systems that compound value.

results.title: The Truth About AI Agents: Workflows Over Hype | Alex Vacca 🧠🛠️ posted on the topic | LinkedIn
results.content: Everyone’s talking about AI agents. Almost no one’s actually using them right. When we started building internal AI agents at ColdIQ, I bought into the hype. Autonomous systems. Self-learning agents. “The future of business.” After months of building, breaking, and rebuilding, I realized most “AI agents” are just really well-designed workflows. And that’s not a bad thing. Here’s the breakdown 👇 1️⃣ Non-agentic workflows (where you should start) You ask ChatGPT to write an email, it writes the email. Done. One input → LLM Request → One output. That's it. Examples from our daily ops: - Prospect research: Input LinkedIn profile → Output enriched contact data - Email copywriting: Input campaign brief → Output personalized sequences - Call summarization: Input transcript → Output action [...] Everyone’s talking about AI agents. Almost no one’s actually using them right. When we started building internal AI agents at ColdIQ, I bought into the hype. Autonomous systems. Self-learning agents. “The future of business.” After months of building, breaking, and rebuilding, I realized most “AI agents” are just really well-designed workflows. And that’s not a bad thing. Here’s the breakdown 👇 1️⃣ Non-agentic workflows (where you should start) You ask ChatGPT to write an email, it writes the email. Done. One input → LLM Request → One output. That's it. Examples from our daily ops: - Prospect research: Input LinkedIn profile → Output enriched contact data - Email copywriting: Input campaign brief → Output personalized sequences - Call summarization: Input transcript → Output action items [...] are just fancy workflows with better marketing. Everyone's talking about agents that can think and learn like humans. The truth? We're not there yet. Real agents should: - Understand context and make complex decisions - Learn from outcomes and improve over time - Handle unexpected situations without breaking We're building towards this at ColdIQ, but honestly? The technology isn't quite there yet for most business use cases. The truth about AI agents: 99% of what people call "AI agents" are just well-designed workflows. And that's actually good news - workflows are reliable, predictable, and profitable. 1. Start simple 2. Build workflows that solve real problems 3. Then gradually add complexity Most companies wanna jump straight to "AI agents" and end up with broken, unreliable systems.
